posts.author: wler
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** A ring laser. I have read once before that a ring laser setup can even make a dye laser single frequency. How does a ring setup where the light travels only in one direction through the lasing medium enable one single wavelength to win?

Because there are no standing waves like in an ordinary resonator; for the latter, the resonance condition is satified by a large number of longitudinal modes, and those which happen to lie within the gain curve of the lasing medium, will be excited. This effectively reduces the coherence lentgh. Then there are other effects like "spatial hole burning", which makes it it easier for competing modes to become excited. 

This is not so for a ring laser - there are no multiple resonance modes at all to start with, and there is no spatial hole burning but rather a "winner takes all" principle at work. There is only one thing to care about, namely there will be also a wave running in the opposite direction, which takes away 50% of the power; unles one makes it hard for this mode to come up (like using an acoustic modulator or somethng else).

Surely single mode operation can alse be achieved by an ordinary resonator, but things like etalons and other tricks are necessary. Unless one is taking care of this, there is practicaly no way to have single mode operation, and this applies to basically all DPSS lasers that are not specifically designed for single longitudinal mode.

PS: here's a brief [movie](http://argonholo.webhop.net/laser/pics/633modedrift.AVI) (3.8MB) I did a few days ago, showing how a few longitudinal modes of a HeNE laser drift while it warms up (the lower trace shows a 10x zoom). I plan to do more of such investigations esp for diode and DPSS lasers.

posts.author: Bastian_S
posts.content_md: in standing wave resonators there is something called spatial hole burning. The standing wave leaves population inversion at its nodes untouched. The next longitudinal mode doesnt have its nodes at the same position and sees inversion left by the other and starts oscillating too. in a ring setup there is no standing wave and therefore one single mode CAN dominate the others. /edit wler was faster ... /edit 2 AFAIK there are multiple resonaces in a ring laser too, spaced c/l ( l= ring length) apart if I remember correctly.

easiest way to force one direction would be self injection locking : the two ring directions will leave your OC under different angles. just take a mirror and reflect one direction back in itself into the resonator. 

Nevertheless, forget the ring, its extremely tough to build.

And forget diode pumping a pulsed holography laser. You wont be able to pay pump diodes that have enough peak power. If you want lets say 10 mJ ( which is still waaay to less) in 5 ns your laser has a peak power of 2 kW. Your pump might not need the same peak power because you can pump longer than the laser pulse but on the other hand you dont have 100% eficiency from pump power to green, so youll need a pump diode in the kW regime.

Id go for Bill Jensens approach, it seems to work quite well, although its probably not single frequency.

40 plus years ago I remember growing my own crystals of ammonium diHydrogen phosphate (ADP)to make a piezoelectric resonator. I just left a saturated solution in a dust free place for weeks.

I learned which direction to cleave my best looking crystal in from a book by a guy called Mason. "Can I make a chemical fluid filled q-switch at home?"

Yes I think you could do that.

I acquired a cylindrical 5 cm long glass cell with parallel windows about 2 cm diameter from lab equipment suppliers . It was made with 2 filling tubes with mini stoppers. I filled it with trichloroethylene in which I had dissolved a small amount of a special dye I got from Eastman-Kodak at that time (~12 yrs ago) The dye contained Ni , I could post you a bit if you are seriously interested in doing it. Any good hydrophobic solvent of that type would do I think .(eg xylene).

beam profile patterns you got from it were often quite weird and wonderful

particularly if you were doing multiple 0.1 sec pulses. (I suppose this was caused by thermal effects in the liquid.Such variabilities were ultimately not helpful in my work here so it was replaced by the crystal system.)

Did you leave the silane treated slides open to the air for several hours ?

The silane layer needs to "hydolyse" with ambient humidity so that it forms SiOH groups which then adhere to the similar bonds on the glass surface. If you don't give it time to hydrolyse you might get the trouble you describe. Incidentally I now find that I can get at least as good a bond by using only o.2 ml in 100 cc acetone. It being only a surface effect of course. 

Using a long sheet of glass and the Dave Battin coating method would make things easier for you I think.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I again will have to state my proceedures as I have never had emulsion lifts. I have used both plain gelatin and full emulsions.

I take my glass, new or previously coated, and place in a 3% solution of Hydrochloric acid (readily available in low concentrationfrom hardware store as Muriatic Acid) in a plastic sealable container. I leave there overnight or longer, sometimes weeks. Basically, if a hologram is not to be saved I put it and store it in the solution. When I am cooking my gelatin, I take the glass out of the container one by one and scrub it with a plastic wool (used for Teflon pans) while wearing rubber gloves. And then place in a tray under running tap water. When I have done all the plates I want to do I take each of the plates again and scrub them with the plastic wool again under running water and plate in a 45 degree angle drying rack. Before all the water has evaportated off the glass I take each and still wearing rubber gloves (to keep oils off from the hands) dry the plates with a 1/4 sheet of paper towel. I use one sheet of paper towel in my left hand to hold the edges of the glass and a second sheet in my right hand balled up. I rub the glass across and up and down and turn the balled up towel until it is felt and heard that there is no more moisture on the glass. Then I do the other side. I place the glass horizonally on a paper towel layed out on the work surface. Depending on the coating thickness I want the my ambient room temperature, I may coat directly or place the plates in an oven to warm (up to 120F.) By the time I am done, the gelatin mixure has cooked. At this point I take the glass, hit it with a blast of air from canned air (for computers) and coat. 

Whether plain gel or fully mixed emulsion, I have never had emulsion lift. When drying with the balled up paper towel I can feel different textures to the opposite sides of the glass. But no matter which side I use, I still do not experience emulsion lifts.

It may be worth a try.

I dont think the developer makes much difference to your "no-show" result. TEA on its own should be fine as sensitizer so that leaves the question of the dye. Perhaps too much has come out of solution. Try adding more alcohol to the LiBr bath and stirr it round , the dye should go back into solution. 

Another thought, Did you blow dry the plate so that it was not swollen before you put it in the Br- bath? --Otherwise the AgNO3

migrates out faster than the LiBr migrates in.

------------------------------------------

A good Developer is :

Solution A

 40 g ascorbic acid 

6 g “Metol” 4-methylaminophenol 

Made up to 1 litre in distilled or deionized water

Solution B 

100 g anhydrous sodium carbonate ( Na2CO)3 

30 g Sodium hydroxide (NaOH). 

Made up to 1 litre in distilled or deionized water

Mix equal volumes of A and B for the developer.

The mixture should be used in a plastic dish with an identical dish floating on the top so that there is a minimal air gap. If you use it like this the same developer can be used again and again for many days (depending on how much usage of course) otherwise this developer left in an open dish is more vulnerable to oxidation from the air than standard developers because it deliberately does not contain sulfite ions. So the time the developer spends exposed to the air is low when you use a floating dish and it is only while immersing your plates or taking them out that it is fully open to the air. Unmixed solutions A and B keep indefinitely. A yellowing or browning of solution A is OK . ( Badly oxidized solution A is BLACK).

Jeff

With the old relatively fast Agfa 8E75HD I used to find this trouble if I left "TEAed" plates for a week before exposure. or very slow development of AgBr grains which would happen in any developer given enough time. .

I have been pleasantly surprised to find though that I can get away with using BB640 plates that had been 5%TEAed several months previously! and not even refrigerated.

That said, I have not noticed any particular extra fogging from TEA in the emulsion for BB and Ultimate emulsions when developed with metol/ascorbic acid at my low basement temperatures (~10C). Even so, when using TEA, I superstitiously continue to pre-rinse in distilled water before developing - it can't hurt (can it?), and I speculate that for very hard emulsions, a presoak could help the developer to penetrate the thickness of the emulsion more quickly for more even depth development...

Hans,

Are you sure that your emulsion is between 5um and 10 um?

A 10 um spacer will give a 10 um wet-gelatin layer.

The thickness of the dry gelatin will be about 15%, so 1.5 microns.

This is too thin, and will give no, or a very weak hologram.

I would suggest to develope one plate with the lights on.

The maximum achievable density will be so reached

and you can check if the reason for your problem is underexposure,

or a bad emulsion.

Last week, I have coated a plate.

I cut a small piece and tested it for Dmax. I measured a Dmax=1.6 only.

(... I have to investigate the reasons!)

I exposed the rest @633 nm, in a denisyuk setup.

The plate reached a D=1.2

Although weak, the hologram is very clear, without any noise, and with some bright spots

Is there nothing that can be taken as read?Yes it's typical. Even if a particular statement about processing was correct when it was written, materials, contaminants, and processing environments change. Nothing should be taken as Gospel. That said, I have not noticed any particular extra fogging from TEA in the emulsion for BB and Ultimate emulsions when developed with metol/ascorbic acid at my low basement temperatures (~10C). Even so, when using TEA, I superstitiously continue to pre-rinse in distilled water before developing - it can't hurt (can it?), and I speculate that for very hard emulsions, a presoak could help the developer to penetrate the thickness of the emulsion more quickly for more even depth development...Perhaps other developers are more sensitive to TEA?

Yes I have now checked this out using cut up BB640 plates.

There is no sign what so ever of any additional fogging occurring if 10%

TEA is left on the plate when it goes into developer, compared to the same plate with the TEA washed off under running tap water for a minute before being put in the same developer. Furthermore lower down

on that page quoted by Michael, Graham goes on to recommend using an unexposed chip of plate to be put in the dev with your hologram and then when this chip has gone gray then it is time to take the hologram out .

"Nothing will be gained by leaving in longer." he says.

In practice today if you worked like that then Slavich stuff should'nt be developed at all ! because unexposed plate goes gray almost at once ...

if you are lucky ...... usually I find they go much darker. The new Fuji material also I find has a certain fog level. However let's get this in some perspective . In James' Theory of the Photographic Process some low inherent fog level is considered normal . Developers of the high contrast type which we require are a compromise to bring out the best contrast between the exposed and unexposed parts with respect to a short development time. If the unexposed bits did not have a slight fog level at all it would indicate the developer was unlikely to be satisfactory to get high fringe contrast.

 THE real question is does this fog effect get much worse after plates have had a relatively short storage time ? Compared to photographic materials with vastly greater ASA values , holographic material should be able to be kept for years in really dry conditions without damned refrigeration being necessary. I have 25 years old Agfa 8E 75 

which makes a pretty good job of it. 

jeff

posts.content_md:
> **Tom B.:** jeff-blyth wrote:The new Fuji material also I find has a certain fog level.Yes, I noticed this on unexposed areas but I wasn't at all alarmed since it cleared very rapidly in the bleach (a few seconds) compared to exposed areas. I wondered if it might be due to residual sensitivity to the safelight I was using (OptiLeds amber) when chopping up the sheets and setting up. Which reminds me I should do a safelight test...Re my earlier statement about water presoak before developing possibly promoting more even development, I now realize that the argument could be turned around: that developer would more rapidly penetrate dry thirsty gelatin than it would diffuse into sopping wet gelatin. I dunno - I kind of suspect that it makes little or no discernable difference and my presoak routine is a meaningless, though comforting, ritual.

No your ritual routine is correct from a purist point of view. There are large osmotic pressure forces at work between virtually pure water saturating the emulsion and high ionic concentrations in the developer outside. Over the ~10 micron thickness of the emulsion these osmotic pressure forces act faster than it would take dry emulsion to imbibe developer solution and swell up. With very fast development times I have found that by looking at the absorption hologram in just silver without any bleaching , a reflection hologram can look fine on the emulsion side but then you see almost nothing through the glass side.

----In other words the development is so uneven that the back end of the hologram against the glass has perhaps got no fringe structure . Longer development time would have sorted this but then the front of the hologram would be getting over developed ie your dark fringes are starting to develop up. So you can have a catch up problem and a more broad band result because of unequal fringe thicknesses. But generally with moderately short dev times it does not seem to make much difference if you do just put your dry plate in the dev withou the presoak.

jeff
